source_pages.title: Organize your resources with management groups
Regulatory Compliance details for FedRAMP Moderate - Azure Policy

questions.question: A regulated bank deploys a storage account in a subscription that has an Azure Policy assignment with a Deny effect for storage SKUs outside an approved list. A subscription Owner tries to create a Premium storage account that is not on the approved list. What happens, and why?
options: The deployment is blocked because Azure Policy evaluates resource state against business rules regardless of who makes the change
The deployment succeeds because an Owner outranks policy enforcement
The deployment succeeds but is flagged only at the next 24-hour compliance cycle
The deployment is blocked only if the Owner lacks the Resource Policy Contributor role
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Azure Policy ensures resource state is compliant with business rules without concern for who made the change, and even an individual with access to perform an action is blocked if the result is a non-compliant resource. B is wrong — RBAC permission does not override policy Deny. C is wrong — Deny is enforced at create/update time, not only at the 24-hour cycle. D is wrong — the Resource Policy Contributor role governs managing policy objects, not bypassing enforcement.
questions.source_quote: Even if an individual has access to perform an action, if the result is a non-compliant resource, Azure Policy still blocks the create or update.

questions.question: A security team wants to stop users from manually deleting a critical Key Vault, but allow automated deployment pipelines to delete and recreate lower-environment vaults. Which Azure Policy mechanism fits this requirement?
options: An Audit effect policy scoped to the production resource group
An identity-based policy using requestContext().identity to block delete requests initiated by a user from any client
A Deny effect policy on the management group covering all vaults
A role assignment removing Contributor from all users
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Azure Policy can base enforcement on who makes the request via requestContext().identity — for example, blocking users from manually deleting critical resources. A is wrong — Audit only logs, it never blocks. C is wrong — a blanket Deny would also block the pipelines. D is wrong — RBAC changes are not policy, and removing Contributor would break legitimate pipeline and admin work.
questions.source_quote: Block users from manually deleting critical resources by adding a condition that checks whether the request was initiated by a user from any client.

questions.question: An enterprise has 400 subscriptions under a management group hierarchy. A new policy initiative for ISO 27001 is assigned at the root management group. A subscription owner in a child subscription claims the initiative does not apply because they never accepted it. What is true?
options: The initiative applies only to subscriptions created after the assignment
The initiative applies only after each subscription owner approves the assignment
The initiative applies to all descendant subscriptions by inheritance and the subscription owner cannot alter it
The initiative applies only if the subscription trusts a different Microsoft Entra tenant
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Governance conditions applied to a management group cascade by inheritance to all associated subscriptions, and the resource or subscription owner cannot alter the security policy. B is wrong — inheritance is automatic, no per-subscription acceptance is needed. A is wrong — assignments apply to existing and new resources in scope. D is wrong — all subscriptions within a management group must trust the same Microsoft Entra tenant.
questions.source_title: Organize your resources with management groups
questions.source_quote: When you organize subscriptions into management groups, the governance conditions that you apply cascade by inheritance to all associated subscriptions.

questions.question: A company is designing its management group hierarchy. The architects propose seven levels of management groups below the root, with one subscription having two parent management groups for dual reporting. Which design constraint blocks this plan?
options: The root management group counts toward the six levels, so only five are allowed
A directory supports only 100 management groups, so seven levels is impossible
Subscriptions cannot be placed under management groups at all
A management group tree supports up to six levels of depth, and each management group and subscription can support only one parent
questions.explanation: Correct: D. A management group tree supports up to six levels of depth (not including the root or subscription level), and each management group and subscription can have only one parent. B is wrong — a single directory supports 10,000 management groups. C is wrong — subscriptions are the children of management groups by design. A is wrong — the six-level limit explicitly excludes the root level and the subscription level.
questions.source_title: Organize your resources with management groups
questions.source_quote: A management group tree can support up to six levels of depth. This limit doesn't include the root level or the subscription level. Each management group and subscription can support only one parent.

questions.question: A tenant administrator wants a policy that applies to every current and future subscription in the tenant, including ones created next year. Where should the assignment be scoped, and what is the key risk of that choice?
options: At the root management group, but any assignment there applies to all resources in the directory so it must be must-have only
At each subscription individually, because root assignments expire after one year
At the resource group level, because root assignments cannot contain policies
At the management group level only for subscriptions that already exist
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The root management group allows global policies and role assignments at the directory level, new subscriptions automatically default to it, but anything assigned on the root applies to the entire hierarchy so it should be must-have only. B is wrong — root assignments do not expire. C is wrong — resource groups are below subscriptions and cannot cover future subscriptions. D is wrong — inheritance covers future subscriptions folded under the hierarchy.
questions.source_title: Organize your resources with management groups
questions.source_quote: Any assignment of user access or policy on the root management group applies to all resources within the directory. User access and policy assignments should be must have only at this scope.

questions.question: A global administrator has no access to the root management group and cannot assign a tenant-wide policy. What is the correct way to gain that access?
options: Ask another Global Administrator to grant Owner directly, since Global Administrators have default root access
Elevate access to manage all Azure subscriptions and management groups to the User Access Administrator role of the root group
Create a new management group above the root
Assign the Contributor role at the subscription level, which inherits upward to the root
questions.explanation: Correct: B. No one has default access to the root management group; Microsoft Entra Global Administrators are the only users who can elevate themselves to gain access, initially by elevating to User Access Administrator of the root group. A is wrong — Global Administrators do not have default root access. C is wrong — the root management group cannot be moved and nothing sits above it. D is wrong — RBAC inherits downward, never upward.
questions.source_title: Organize your resources with management groups
questions.source_quote: No one has default access to the root management group. Microsoft Entra Global Administrators are the only users who can elevate themselves to gain access.

questions.question: A hospital's existing virtual machines are non-compliant with a new policy requiring diagnostic logs to be sent to a Log Analytics workspace. The policy uses deployIfNotExists. A remediation task is created. What must be true for remediation to succeed?
options: Any Reader on the subscription can trigger remediation
The VMs must be deleted and recreated, because deployIfNotExists cannot remediate existing resources
The policy's managed identity needs enough permissions to create or update the targeted resources
Remediation runs automatically with no identity, because the policy itself performs the deployment
questions.explanation: Correct: C. The managed identity of a deployIfNotExists or modify policy assignment needs enough permissions to create or update targeted resources, and a User Access Administrator is necessary to grant the managed identity those permissions. B is wrong — deployIfNotExists exists precisely to bring existing resources to compliance through remediation. A is wrong — Reader has only read operations. D is wrong — deployments are performed under the managed identity, not anonymously.
questions.source_quote: The managed identity of a deployIfNotExists or modify policy assignment needs enough permissions to create or update targeted resources.

questions.question: A team rolls out a new Deny policy for disallowed resource types on a Friday afternoon. By Monday, autoscaling scripts are failing. What does Microsoft's own guidance say they should have done first?
options: Assigned the policy at the resource level so autoscaling bypasses it
Scoped the Deny policy to the root management group so it applies everywhere at once
Used a modify effect instead, which never interferes with automation
Started with an audit or auditIfNotExists effect to track how the policy affects resources before using an enforcement effect
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Microsoft recommends starting with an audit or auditIfNotExists effect instead of an enforcement effect to track how the policy definition affects resources, noting that an enforcement effect might hinder existing autoscaling automation. B is wrong — root scoping would widen the blast radius. C is wrong — modify alters resources and can also interfere. A is wrong — policy assigned at a parent scope still evaluates resources below it.
questions.source_quote: Start with an audit or auditIfNotExists effect instead of an enforcement (deny, modify, deployIfNotExists) effect to track how your policy definition affects the resources in your environment.

questions.question: An auditor asks when Azure Policy re-evaluates a resource that has not changed. Which evaluation trigger applies to an unchanged, already-deployed resource?
options: The standard compliance evaluation cycle that occurs once every 24 hours
Only when the resource is deleted and recreated
Only when a user manually triggers an on-demand scan from the portal
Every 15 minutes, as part of the near-real-time evaluation loop
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Resources are evaluated when created or updated, when a scope gets a new assignment, when an assigned policy is updated, and on the standard compliance evaluation cycle that occurs once every 24 hours. B is wrong — deletion is not an evaluation trigger. C is wrong — manual scans are possible but are not the standard cycle for unchanged resources. D is wrong — there is no 15-minute standard cycle; the standard cycle is 24 hours.
questions.source_quote: The standard compliance evaluation cycle that occurs once every 24 hours.

questions.question: A company assigns a policy initiative for PCI DSS at the management group level. A compliance dashboard shows 100% compliant. The CISO asks whether this proves full PCI DSS compliance. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, a 100% Azure Policy score is accepted as full PCI DSS attestation
No, Compliant in Azure Policy refers only to the policy definitions themselves and does not ensure full compliance with all requirements of a control
Yes, but only if the initiative was assigned at the root management group
No, because policy initiatives cannot map to PCI DSS at all
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Microsoft states there is often not a one-to-one or complete match between a control and one or more policies, so Compliant in Azure Policy refers only to the policy definitions themselves and does not ensure full compliance with all requirements of a control; some controls have no policy definitions at all. A is wrong — the dashboard is a partial view, not attestation. C is wrong — scope does not change the partial-mapping caveat. D is wrong — built-in initiatives exist for PCI DSS and other standards.
questions.source_title: Regulatory Compliance details for FedRAMP Moderate - Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: Compliant in Azure Policy refers only to the policy definitions themselves; this doesn't ensure you're fully compliant with all requirements of a control.

questions.question: A financial services firm must demonstrate control coverage for FedRAMP Moderate, including a control that requires at most three subscription owners. Which Azure Policy mechanism enforces this, and what effect does the built-in definition use?
options: A manual attestation workflow, because ownership limits cannot be expressed in policy
An RBAC deny assignment, because policy cannot inspect role assignments
The FedRAMP Moderate built-in initiative, which includes a definition recommending a maximum of 3 owners, using AuditIfNotExists
A Blueprint lock, which is the only mechanism that limits subscription owners
questions.explanation: Correct: C. The FedRAMP Moderate initiative maps controls to policy definitions, including the control that a maximum of 3 owners should be designated for a subscription, with effect AuditIfNotExists. A is wrong — the control is implemented as a policy definition. B is wrong — deny assignments are a lock mechanism, not how this control is expressed. D is wrong — Blueprints are retiring and were never the mechanism for this control.
questions.source_title: Regulatory Compliance details for FedRAMP Moderate - Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: A maximum of 3 owners should be designated for your subscription.

questions.question: An organization built its environment governance on Azure Blueprints, relying on Blueprint locks to prevent changes to governed resources. It is now December 2026 and no migration has started. What is the most urgent consequence they face on January 31, 2027?
options: All resources deployed by Blueprints will be deleted
Only new Blueprint definitions stop being creatable; existing locks remain forever
Blueprints will continue read-only indefinitely with locks intact
All Blueprint Locks (Deny Assignments) are removed and definitions and assignments are deleted, so lock-based enforcement is gone
questions.explanation: Correct: D. After January 31, 2027 Blueprints can no longer be modified, all Blueprint Locks (Deny Assignments) are removed, and definitions and assignments are removed from the portal, while deployed resources remain in place. A is wrong — resources remain and inherit parent RBAC. C is wrong — the service is fully retired, not read-only indefinitely. B is wrong — new definitions already stopped in July 2026 and locks are removed at retirement.
questions.source_quote: After January 31, 2027, Blueprints can no longer be modified, all Blueprint Locks (Deny Assignments) are removed, and Blueprint Definitions and Assignments are removed from the portal.

questions.question: A team migrating off Azure Blueprints wants to preserve the same lock behavior that prevented out-of-band changes to governed resources. What does Microsoft recommend?
options: Manage the workload under a Deployment Stack and configure deny assignments on the stack
Export the Blueprint and rely on standard Azure resource locks alone
Recreate the Blueprint as a policy initiative, which provides identical deny assignments
Move the resources to a new subscription, which inherits Blueprint locks
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Microsoft recommends migrating to Deployment Stacks, which provide the equivalent management-plane protection including deny settings, and advises migrating managed resources to a Deployment Stack and configuring deny assignments to preserve the same lock behavior. B is wrong — plain resource locks are only an acceptable limited approach for a tenant on a near-term decommissioning timeline. C is wrong — policy initiatives enforce resource properties; they do not provide Blueprint-style deny assignments. D is wrong — moving resources does not carry Blueprint locks, which are removed at retirement.
questions.source_quote: Manage the workload under a Deployment Stack. Deployment Stacks provide the equivalent management-plane protection, including deny settings, in a supported, forward-going service.

questions.question: A company has not exported its Blueprint definitions and assignments. It is February 2027. What is the state of those artifacts?
options: They are recoverable from the portal recycle bin for 90 days
They were permanently deleted at retirement and cannot be recovered
They were automatically converted to Deployment Stacks
They remain in the portal in read-only mode
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Any definitions, versions, and assignments not exported before January 31, 2027 are permanently deleted at retirement and cannot be recovered. A is wrong — there is no recycle-bin recovery. C is wrong — migration is a manual re-authoring exercise, not automatic conversion. D is wrong — the portal access is removed at retirement.
questions.source_quote: Any definitions, versions, and assignments you haven't exported are permanently deleted at retirement and can't be recovered, so export anything you want to keep before January 31, 2027.

questions.question: An architect must explain to executives why Azure Blueprints and Azure Policy are not interchangeable. Which distinction is correct?
options: Blueprints enforce rules and Policies only deploy resources
A policy packages role assignments and ARM templates, while a Blueprint only audits tags

A Blueprint is a package for composing standards and patterns that can be reused to maintain consistency, while a policy is a default-allow and explicit-deny system focused on resource properties during deployment and for existing resources
They are identical; Blueprints are simply the new name for policy initiatives
questions.explanation: Correct: C. A Blueprint is a package or container for composing focus-specific sets of standards, patterns, and requirements that can be reused, while a policy is a default allow and explicit deny system focused on resource properties during deployment and for already existing resources. B reverses the two. A is wrong — policies enforce, Blueprints package artifacts including policies. D is wrong — they are distinct services, and Blueprints is retiring while Policy continues.
questions.source_quote: Azure Policy evaluates state by examining properties on resources that are represented in Resource Manager and properties of some Resource Providers.

questions.question: A CISO wants one assignment that enforces allowed locations, allowed VM SKUs, and mandatory diagnostic logging across 60 subscriptions, and wants to add a fourth rule later without creating new assignments. What should they create?
options: Three separate policy definitions assigned individually to each subscription
A single custom RBAC role with all three rules encoded as permissions
One Blueprint per subscription, since initiatives cannot group policies
One initiative definition containing the policy definitions, assigned once, so later definitions can be added to the initiative without increasing assignments
questions.explanation: Correct: D. An initiative definition is a collection of policy definitions tailored toward one overarching goal; Microsoft recommends creating and assigning initiatives even with a single policy so definitions can be added later without increasing the number of assignments, and after an initiative assignment is created, added policies become part of its assignments. A is wrong — it multiplies assignments by 60 subscriptions times 3 policies. C is wrong — initiatives, not Blueprints, group policies, and Blueprints is retiring. B is wrong — RBAC controls who can act, not resource properties like location or SKU.
questions.source_quote: We recommend creating and assigning initiative definitions even if starting with a single policy definition. This method enables you to add policy definitions to the initiative later without increasing the number of assignments to manage.

questions.question: A policy definition is created at a management group, but the team wants the assignment scoped to one child subscription only. Is this supported, and what is the recommended pattern?
options: Yes, create definitions at higher levels such as the management group and create the assignment at the next child level
No, definitions and assignments must share the same scope
Yes, but only if the definition is recreated at the subscription level
No, assignments can only be scoped above the definition
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Microsoft recommends creating definitions at higher levels such as the management group or subscription level, then creating the assignment at the next child level; a definition at a management group can be assigned down to a subscription or resource group within it. B is wrong — definition and assignment scopes may differ. C is wrong — no recreation is needed. D is wrong — assignments are scoped at or below the definition, not above.
questions.source_quote: If you create a definition at a management group, the assignment can be scoped down to a subscription or resource group within that management group.

questions.question: A developer with the Contributor role tries to create a new Azure Policy assignment. A colleague with the Resource Policy Contributor role succeeds. Why did the Contributor fail?
options: Contributor lacks read access to policy objects
Contributor cannot create or update definitions and assignments, though it can trigger remediation; Resource Policy Contributor includes most policy operations
Contributor can only manage policies at the resource group scope
Resource Policy Contributor is the only role that can read policy compliance data
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Contributor might trigger resource remediation but cannot create or update definitions and assignments, while the Resource Policy Contributor role includes most Azure Policy operations. A is wrong — Contributor has access to all read Azure Policy operations. C is wrong — scope is not the issue. D is wrong — all roles over a scope can read policy objects; definitions, initiatives, and assignments are visible to all users.
questions.source_quote: Contributor might trigger resource remediation, but can't create or update definitions and assignments.

questions.question: A security engineer argues that assigning the Owner role to the data team will also enforce that they only deploy resources to approved regions. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Owner already enforces region restrictions by default
Owner cannot be assigned at the management group scope
Azure RBAC focuses on managing user actions at different scopes, while Azure Policy evaluates resource state; RBAC alone does not enforce resource properties
Region enforcement requires the User Access Administrator role, not Owner
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Azure RBAC focuses on managing user actions at different scopes; Azure Policy evaluates state by examining resource properties. The combination provides full scope control — RBAC alone never enforces allowed locations. A is wrong — Owner grants full rights, not restrictions. B is wrong — Owner can be assigned at management group scope. D is wrong — User Access Administrator manages access, not regions.
questions.source_quote: Azure RBAC focuses on managing user actions at different scopes. If control of an action is required based on user information, then Azure RBAC is the correct tool to use.

questions.question: An organization uses Azure Arc to manage on-premises servers. The CISO wants the same allowed-location and tagging policies applied to those servers. What does Azure Policy offer here?
options: Nothing, because Azure Policy only evaluates resources in Azure regions
Arc servers can only be governed by Blueprints, not by policy
Only RBAC applies to Arc-enabled servers; policy requires native Azure resources
Policy-based governance can be extended across different cloud providers and to local datacenters with Azure Arc
questions.explanation: Correct: D. With Azure Arc, policy-based governance can be extended across different cloud providers and even to local datacenters. A is wrong — Arc is precisely the extension mechanism. C is wrong — policy evaluates Arc-enabled resources too. B is wrong — Blueprints is retiring and was never the only governance path for Arc.
questions.source_quote: It's important to recognize that with the introduction of Azure Arc, you can extend your policy-based governance across different cloud providers and even to your local datacenters.

questions.question: A company operates in the EU and must ensure no resources are deployed outside approved regions. Two controls are proposed: an Azure Policy allowed-locations Deny, and a management group policy that limits VM creation regions. Which statement best describes how these interact?
options: Both are policy assignments; the management group assignment inherits down to all nested management groups, subscriptions, and resources
They conflict, so only one can be assigned at a time
The management group policy only applies to VMs, so storage accounts ignore it
Allowed-locations policies cannot use the Deny effect
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A policy applied to a management group that limits regions is applied to all nested management groups, subscriptions, and resources; assignments at different scopes compose rather than conflict. B is wrong — multiple assignments can coexist. C is wrong — the example is about VM creation, but allowed-locations policies apply to resource deployment generally. D is wrong — Allowed Locations is a built-in Deny policy.
questions.source_title: Organize your resources with management groups
questions.source_quote: You can apply a policy to a management group that limits the regions available for virtual machine (VM) creation. This policy would be applied to all nested management groups, subscriptions, and resources.

questions.question: A consultant recommends assigning the VM Contributor role once at a management group instead of scripting RBAC across 40 subscriptions. What is the effect, and what is the limitation?
options: The role grants Owner rights across all subscriptions immediately
The role has no action on the management group itself but inherits to all VMs under it; it does not grant access to non-VM resources
The role applies only to VMs created after the assignment
The role cannot be assigned at management group scope at all
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Moving multiple subscriptions under a management group lets one role assignment inherit to all subscriptions; for example, VM Contributor assigned to a management group has no action on the management group but inherits to all VMs under it. A is wrong — VM Contributor is scoped to VM operations, not Owner. C is wrong — inheritance applies to existing and new VMs. D is wrong — any Azure role can be assigned to a management group.
questions.source_title: Organize your resources with management groups
questions.source_quote: You can assign the Azure role VM Contributor to a management group. This role has no action on the management group but inherits to all VMs under that management group.

questions.question: A custom RBAC role is defined on the Sandbox management group and assigned on two Sandbox subscriptions. An admin tries to move one subscription to the Corp management group and gets an error. What is the cause and the fix?
options: Management groups cannot be moved once created
The subscription has resources, and subscriptions with resources can never move

The move breaks the path from the subscription role assignment to the role definition; remove the assignment before moving, add the subscription to the definition's assignable scope, or widen the scope to the root
The admin lacks Owner on the subscription, which is the only permission needed
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Moving a subscription breaks the relationship between the role assignment and its definition on the Sandbox management group; the documented fixes are removing the assignment before moving, adding the subscription to the assignable scope, or updating assignable scopes to the root management group. B is wrong — subscriptions with resources can move. A is wrong — management groups can be moved with the right permissions. D is wrong — the error is about the definition-assignment path, not Owner.
questions.source_title: Organize your resources with management groups
questions.source_quote: If you try to move one of those subscriptions to be a child of the Corp management group, this breaks the path from subscription role assignment to the role definition for the sandbox management group.

questions.question: A team designs a custom role with DataActions and wants to assign it at the management group scope to enforce data-plane access across all subscriptions. What will they discover?
options: DataActions are automatically converted to Actions at management group scope
DataActions roles can be assigned at any scope including management groups
Only one management group per directory may host a DataActions role
Custom roles with DataActions cannot be assigned at the management group scope
questions.explanation: Correct: D. A documented limitation is that custom roles with DataActions cannot be assigned at the management group scope. B contradicts that limitation. C is wrong — the one-management-group limit applies to assignable scopes in a role definition, not to DataActions. A is wrong — no such conversion exists.
questions.source_title: Organize your resources with management groups
questions.source_quote: Custom roles with DataActions can't be assigned at the management group scope.

questions.question: An enterprise wants new subscriptions to automatically receive governance policies and permissions the moment they are created, with no manual step. Which design delivers this?
options: Use the root management group to assign enterprise-wide security elements, since new subscriptions automatically default to the root management group
Assign policies at the subscription level after each creation via a runbook
Create a Blueprint assignment per subscription, which auto-applies to future subscriptions
Rely on Azure Policy's automatic discovery, which assigns policies to new subscriptions without a scope
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Microsoft recommends using the root management group to assign enterprise-wide security elements that apply to all Azure assets, and new subscriptions automatically default to the root management group when created. B is wrong — it requires a manual or runbook step per subscription. C is wrong — Blueprints is retiring and assignments are per-scope. D is wrong — policy assignments require a scope; there is no automatic assignment without one.
questions.source_quote: Ensure that new subscriptions apply governance elements like policies and permissions as you add them. Use the root management group to assign enterprise-wide security elements that apply to all Azure assets.

questions.question: A company has many subscriptions and wants a single pane to assess compliance of all resources against ISO 27001, HIPAA, and PCI DSS. Which Azure Policy capability provides this, and what does it show?
options: The activity log, which lists every deployment in the last 24 hours
The compliance dashboard, which provides an aggregated view of the overall state of the environment with drill-down to per-resource, per-policy granularity
Azure Advisor, which only shows cost recommendations
The Blueprint assignment view, which is the only place initiatives appear
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Azure Policy's compliance dashboard provides an aggregated view to evaluate the overall state of the environment, with drill-down to per-resource, per-policy granularity, and built-in initiatives exist for standards including FedRAMP High, HIPAA, HITRUST, PCI DSS, and ISO 27001. A is wrong — the activity log is not a compliance aggregation. C is wrong — Advisor covers more than cost but is not the policy compliance dashboard. D is wrong — initiatives are visible in Policy, not only in Blueprints.
questions.source_quote: Through its compliance dashboard, it provides an aggregated view to evaluate the overall state of the environment, with the ability to drill down to the per-resource, per-policy granularity.

questions.question: A healthcare company deploys Azure AI Services and wants to enforce that key-based (local) authentication is disabled so only Microsoft Entra ID can be used. Which governance approach aligns with Microsoft's published regulatory guidance?
options: A Conditional Access policy targeting the AI Services data plane, which is the only supported control
An Azure Policy that deletes any AI Services resource found with keys enabled
A FedRAMP Moderate initiative definition that audits or denies AI Services resources with key access enabled, since the built-in guidance says key access is recommended to be disabled for security
A Blueprint lock, because policy cannot evaluate AI Services resources
questions.explanation: Correct: C. The FedRAMP Moderate initiative includes a definition stating Azure AI Services resources should have key access disabled (disable local authentication), noting that after disabling, Microsoft Entra ID becomes the only access method. B is wrong — policy effects remediate or block, they do not delete resources. A is wrong — Conditional Access governs sign-in, not the resource's local-auth setting. D is wrong — policy can evaluate AI Services resources and Blueprints is retiring.
questions.source_title: Regulatory Compliance details for FedRAMP Moderate - Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: Azure AI Services resources should have key access disabled (disable local authentication). After disabling, Microsoft Entra ID becomes the only access method.

questions.question: An AI team wants to use Azure OpenAI Studio for development and testing while the tenant enforces disabled key access on AI Services. What tension must the governance team resolve?
options: Policy exemptions are not supported for AI Services resources
OpenAI Studio works without keys, so there is no tension
Key access can only be disabled tenant-wide, so development must move to another tenant
Azure OpenAI Studio requires key access and will not function if key access is disabled, so the policy needs a scoped exemption for the dev environment
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Microsoft's own guidance notes Azure OpenAI Studio, typically used in development/testing, requires key access and will not function if key access is disabled — so a blanket deny breaks dev work and needs scoping or an exemption. B contradicts the published note. C is wrong — policy can be scoped and exemptions exist. A is wrong — policy exemptions are a supported mechanism.
questions.source_title: Regulatory Compliance details for FedRAMP Moderate - Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: Azure OpenAI Studio, typically used in development/testing, requires key access and will not function if key access is disabled.

questions.question: A governance lead wants to require MFA before any user can create, update, or delete Azure resources. Which mechanism can enforce this at the resource-management layer?
options: An Azure Policy identity-based rule blocking resource create, update, and delete requests when initiated by a user who doesn't have MFA enabled
An RBAC role assignment, which natively requires MFA for all write operations
A management group lock, which enforces MFA on all child resources
A Blueprint artifact, which is the only place MFA conditions can be expressed
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Azure Policy can require that all users have MFA enabled, blocking resource create, update, and delete requests when initiated by a user without MFA, using the identity context of the request. B is wrong — RBAC grants permission; it does not itself impose MFA on resource operations. C is wrong — locks prevent deletion/modification, they do not check MFA. D is wrong — Blueprints is retiring and MFA conditions belong in policy or Conditional Access, not only in Blueprints.
questions.source_quote: Require that all users have multifactor authentication (MFA) enabled, blocking resource create, update, and delete requests when the request is initiated by a user who doesn't have MFA enabled.

questions.question: A policy assignment at the management group level is showing resources as non-compliant, but the resources themselves are in a subscription, not in the management group. An engineer claims management group assignments cannot evaluate anything. What is true?
options: Management group assignments evaluate the management group object itself, not its resources
Although a policy can be assigned at the management group level, only resources at the subscription or resource group level are evaluated
The assignment is broken; policies must be assigned at the resource level to evaluate anything
Only resources directly in the management group are evaluated, so subscriptions are out of scope
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Microsoft states that although a policy can be assigned at the management group level, only resources at the subscription or resource group level are evaluated — the assignment flows down to the resources. A is wrong — the management group object is not the evaluated target. C is wrong — the assignment is valid. D is wrong — subscriptions are within scope via inheritance.
questions.source_quote: Although a policy can be assigned at the management group level, only resources at the subscription or resource group level are evaluated.

questions.question: A team wants to enforce that every resource carries a cost-center tag, automatically adding a default value when the deployment omits it. Which built-in policy effect and example matches this?
options: Deny, using the Allowed Resource Type policy
AuditIfNotExists, which adds the tag automatically
Modify, using the Add a tag to resources policy, which applies a required tag and its default value if the deploy request doesn't specify it
DeployIfNotExists, which only works for Log Analytics workspaces
questions.explanation: Correct: C. The built-in Add a tag to resources policy uses the Modify effect: it applies a required tag and its default value if the deploy request doesn't specify it. A is wrong — Deny blocks, it does not add tags. B is wrong — AuditIfNotExists only records non-compliance. D is wrong — deployIfNotExists deploys related resources; the tagging example is Modify.
questions.source_quote: Add a tag to resources (Modify): Applies a required tag and its default value if the deploy request doesn't specify it.

questions.question: During Blueprint retirement Phase 2 (October 31, 2026), a team tries to create a new Blueprint assignment for a subscription that was onboarded late. What happens?
options: Assignments can still be created, but definitions cannot
Only delete is disabled; create and update still work
Everything works normally until January 31, 2027
Assignments cannot be created and definitions cannot be created or updated, though delete remains available
questions.explanation: Correct: D. In Phase 2, assignments cannot be created, definitions cannot be created, and definitions cannot be updated; read and delete remain available through Phase 3. A reverses Phase 1 and Phase 2 (in Phase 1 new definitions stopped but assignments could still be created). C is wrong — the phasedown restricts capabilities before retirement. B is wrong — delete remains available, create/update do not.
questions.source_quote: Phase 2 (October 31, 2026): Assignments: No. Definitions: No.

questions.question: An organization with many subscriptions wants to efficiently manage access, policies, and compliance centrally, and to ensure a policy limiting VM regions cannot be bypassed by a subscription owner. Which structure does Microsoft recommend?
options: Organizing subscriptions into management groups and applying governance conditions to the management groups, since all subscriptions within inherit the conditions
Tagging subscriptions by region, because tags enforce inheritance
Creating a separate Microsoft Entra tenant per subscription
Assigning policies at the resource group level in each subscription
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Microsoft states that if an organization has many subscriptions, management groups provide a level of scope above subscriptions, and all subscriptions within a management group automatically inherit the conditions applied to it. B is wrong — tags do not enforce inheritance. C is wrong — management groups require one tenant, and separate tenants fragment governance. D is wrong — resource-group scoping multiplies work and misses new resource groups.
questions.source_quote: Azure management groups provide a level of scope that's above subscriptions. You organize subscriptions into containers called management groups and apply your governance conditions to the management groups. All subscriptions within a management group automatically inherit the conditions applied to the management group.

questions.question: A CISO wants continuous assessment of resource configuration against compliance controls in applied standards and benchmarks. Which service provides this, and how does Azure Policy relate to it?
options: Azure Policy alone performs the assessment; Defender for Cloud only manages firewall rules

Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides continual assessment against compliance controls and best practices in the standards and benchmarks applied; Azure Policy initiatives supply the enforceable definitions
Microsoft Sentinel performs compliance assessment; Policy is unrelated
Azure Monitor assesses compliance; Defender for Cloud only sends alerts
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides a continual assessment of the configuration of resources against compliance controls and best practices in the standards and benchmarks applied in subscriptions, and Azure Policy provides the built-in initiatives for those standards. A is wrong — Defender for Cloud is the assessment service. C is wrong — Sentinel is SIEM/SOAR, not the compliance assessor. D is wrong — Monitor collects logs; it is not the compliance dashboard.
questions.source_quote: Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides a continual assessment of the configuration of your resources against compliance controls and best practices in the standards and benchmarks that you apply in your subscriptions.

questions.question: A regulator asks a bank to prove that its Azure Policy compliance posture is not just a point-in-time screenshot. Which combination best answers the regulator?
options: A single export of the compliance dashboard
A Blueprint assignment report, which is the only auditable record

Continuous evaluation: create/update triggers, assignment lifecycle triggers, and the 24-hour standard cycle, plus bulk remediation records for existing resources and automatic remediation for new ones
RBAC assignment history, which records resource state
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Policy evaluates on resource create/update, new assignments, policy updates, and the 24-hour cycle, and helps bring resources to compliance through bulk remediation for existing resources and automatic remediation for new resources — a continuous, auditable posture. A is wrong — a single screenshot is point-in-time. B is wrong — Blueprints is retiring and is not the compliance record. D is wrong — RBAC history records who could act, not resource compliance state.
questions.source_quote: It also helps to bring your resources to compliance through bulk remediation for existing resources and automatic remediation for new resources.

questions.question: A team manages Azure Policy as code and wants peer review on every change to definitions, initiatives, and assignments. What does Microsoft recommend, and why does it matter for governance?
options: Review only Deny policies; Audit policies cannot cause harm
Edit policies directly in the portal, because code review adds no value for JSON policies
Store policies only in the portal, since exporting them breaks assignments
Manage Azure Policy resources as code with manual reviews on changes to policy definitions, initiatives, and assignments
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Microsoft recommends managing Azure Policy resources as code with manual reviews on changes to definitions, initiatives, and assignments, pointing to Policy-as-Code workflows. B is wrong — portal-only edits bypass review and versioning. C is wrong — policies can be exported and managed as code. A is wrong — even Audit policies shape compliance reporting and later enforcement decisions.
questions.source_quote: Manage Azure Policy resources as code with manual reviews on changes to policy definitions, initiatives, and assignments.

questions.question: A multinational wants a governance hierarchy where the European division's subscriptions inherit EU-only region restrictions, while the global root still enforces MFA-based policy. How should the hierarchy be structured?
options: A root management group for tenant-wide policy, with a nested Europe management group carrying the region restriction that inherits to its descendant subscriptions
One flat management group containing all subscriptions, with region policy assigned per subscription
Two separate tenants, because a hierarchy cannot nest management groups
Assign the region policy at the resource level in each European subscription
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Hierarchies nest management groups up to six levels deep; the root carries global policy and a child management group carries the regional restriction, which cascades to its subscriptions. B is wrong — a flat structure cannot express regional inheritance. C is wrong — one directory has a single hierarchy and nesting is supported. D is wrong — resource-level assignment does not scale and misses future resources.
questions.source_title: Organize your resources with management groups
questions.source_quote: You can build a flexible structure of management groups and subscriptions to organize your resources into a hierarchy for unified policy and access management.

questions.question: An admin needs to move a management group to a new parent. Which permissions are required on the child management group being moved?
options: Only Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/read
Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/write plus Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write and delete, and Microsoft.Management/register/action
Only Owner on the target parent management group
No permissions are needed; management groups can be moved by any Reader
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Moving a child management group requires Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/write, Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete, and Microsoft.Management/register/action on the child (plus write on the target and current parents). A is wrong — read is insufficient. C is wrong — the child and current parent also need write. D is wrong — moves are permission-gated.
questions.source_title: Organize your resources with management groups
questions.source_quote: Microsoft.management/managementgroups/write, Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete, Microsoft.Management/register/action.

questions.question: A company is deciding between using Azure Policy's built-in regulatory initiatives versus writing custom policies for every control. What is the strongest argument for starting with the built-ins?
options: Built-ins automatically grant full regulatory attestation
Custom policies are not supported for regulatory standards
Built-ins are free and already available in the environment for common standards such as FedRAMP High, HIPAA, HITRUST, PCI DSS, and ISO 27001
Built-ins cannot be customized, so they are always faster to deploy
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Policy definitions for common use cases are already available as built-ins, including initiatives for FedRAMP High, HIPAA, HITRUST, PCI DSS, and ISO 27001. B is wrong — custom policies are supported. A is wrong — as established, policy compliance is only a partial view of overall compliance. D is wrong — built-ins support parameters and can be customized via initiatives.
questions.source_quote: Policy definitions for these common use cases are already available in your Azure environment as built-ins to help you get started.

questions.question: A policy definition uses parameters for allowed locations so the same definition can be reused for the US and EU. What is the benefit, and where are parameter values supplied?
options: Parameter values are fixed at definition time and cannot vary by assignment
Parameters eliminate the need for assignments entirely
Parameters only work for initiative definitions, not single policies
Parameters reduce the number of policy definitions you must create; values are passed in when assigning the policy definition
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Parameters simplify management by reducing the number of definitions; you define a parameter such as location and give it different values such as EastUS or WestUS when assigning. B is wrong — assignments are still required. C is wrong — parameters work in policy definitions. A is wrong — varying values per assignment is the point of parameters.
questions.source_quote: Policy parameters help simplify your policy management by reducing the number of policy definitions you must create. Then you can reuse that policy definition for different scenarios by passing in different values when assigning the policy definition.

questions.question: A government agency's Blueprint definitions are stored at a management group but not assigned to any subscription. The team uses the View Impacted Blueprints Resources page to find them before migration. What will they observe?
options: The view lists impact by subscription, so Blueprint definitions saved at a management group that aren't assigned to any subscription don't appear in it
The view lists all definitions regardless of assignment
The view only lists resources deployed by Blueprints, not definitions
The view is unavailable until after retirement
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The impacted-resources view lists impact by subscription, so Blueprint definitions saved at a management group that are not assigned to any subscription do not appear in it — the team must also check the Blueprints portal, which lists management-group definitions. B contradicts the documented behavior. C is wrong — the view is about impacted Blueprint resources including definitions. D is wrong — the view exists before retirement to support migration.
questions.source_quote: This view lists impact by subscription, so blueprint definitions saved at a management group that aren't assigned to any subscription don't appear in it.

questions.question: A tenant is scheduled for decommissioning in three months, well before the Blueprint retirement date matters for its workloads. What migration approach does Microsoft consider acceptable for this tenant?
options: No action is needed at all, because the tenant will be gone

A limited export plus standard Azure resource locks approach is acceptable when the tenant itself is on a near-term decommissioning timeline, though Deployment Stacks remain recommended for workloads that outlive retirement
A full Deployment Stack migration is mandatory even for tenants being decommissioned
The tenant must be migrated to a new tenant first
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Microsoft states a limited export + standard Azure resource locks approach is acceptable when the tenant is on a near-term decommissioning timeline, but recommends Deployment Stacks for any workload that outlives retirement. A is wrong — export is still needed to preserve artifacts. C is wrong — full migration is recommended, not mandatory, for a decommissioning tenant. D is wrong — no tenant migration is required.
questions.source_quote: A limited export + standard Azure resource locks approach is acceptable when the tenant itself is on a near-term decommissioning timeline, but Microsoft recommends Deployment Stacks for any workload that outlives the retirement.

questions.question: A SOC wants policy enforcement to also block specific actions on resources, not just evaluate their properties — for example, blocking users from deleting critical resources. Which effect and capability provides this?
options: The Audit effect, which blocks actions and logs them
The Modify effect, which deletes resources that violate policy
The DenyAction effect, which can block certain actions on resources, combined with identity-aware policy evaluation
RBAC deny assignments, which are part of Azure Policy
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Azure Policy through the DenyAction effect can block certain actions on resources, and policy evaluates identity-based actions via request context. A is wrong — Audit only logs. B is wrong — Modify alters resource properties, it does not block actions. D is wrong — deny assignments are a separate lock mechanism, not a policy effect.
questions.source_quote: Azure Policy through DenyAction effect can also block certain actions on resources.

questions.question: An organization assigns a Deny policy for disallowed resource types at the management group, but excludes one sandbox subscription. A developer in the sandbox deploys a disallowed resource type and it succeeds. A developer in a production subscription tries the same and is blocked. What explains this?
options: The exclusion also removed the policy from production
The sandbox subscription is in a different tenant, so policy cannot reach it
Deny policies only apply to production subscriptions by default
The assignment applies to all resources within the Resource Manager scope of that assignment, and subscopes can be excluded
questions.explanation: Correct: D. An assignment applies to all resources within its Resource Manager scope, and subscopes can be excluded if necessary — the sandbox exclusion is working as designed. B is wrong — all subscriptions in a management group trust the same tenant. C is wrong — there is no production-only default. A is wrong — the production block proves the policy is still active there.
questions.source_quote: The assignment applies to all resources within the Resource Manager scope of that assignment. Subscopes can be excluded, if necessary.

questions.question: A company wants governance for AI workloads that covers both the AI service configuration and the data the models can access. Which combination reflects Microsoft's published guidance?
options: Disable local authentication on Azure AI Services so Entra ID is the only access method, and use sensitivity labels plus DLP to govern the data
Use only Conditional Access, because policy cannot evaluate AI Services
Store model keys in application code for performance, and rely on network isolation alone
Use Blueprint locks for AI governance, since policy initiatives exclude AI resources
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Published FedRAMP guidance recommends disabling key access on Azure AI Services so Entra ID becomes the only access method, and sensitivity labels with encryption and DLP govern data wherever it lives or travels. B is wrong — policy can evaluate AI Services resources. C is wrong — storing keys in code violates Key Vault centralization guidance. D is wrong — Blueprints is retiring and policy initiatives do include AI Services definitions.
questions.source_title: Regulatory Compliance details for FedRAMP Moderate - Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: Azure AI Services resources should have key access disabled (disable local authentication) for security. After disabling, Microsoft Entra ID becomes the only access method.

questions.question: An auditor notes that a FedRAMP Moderate initiative shows several controls with Manual, Disabled policy definitions. What does this mean for the organization's compliance claim?
options: Those controls are automatically compliant because they are listed in the initiative
Those controls are not assessed by policy at all; compliance in Azure Policy is only a partial view and manual controls need separate evidence
Manual definitions are evaluated the same as automated ones
Disabled definitions are still enforced in Audit mode
questions.explanation: Correct: B. The initiative mapping notes many controls are implemented with Manual, Disabled definitions, and the standard includes controls not addressed by any policy definitions — so policy compliance is only a partial view of overall compliance status. A is wrong — listing is not compliance. C is wrong — Manual means human evidence, not automated evaluation. D is wrong — Disabled means the definition is not evaluated.
questions.source_title: Regulatory Compliance details for FedRAMP Moderate - Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: In addition, the compliance standard includes controls that aren't addressed by any Azure Policy definitions at this time. Therefore, compliance in Azure Policy is only a partial view of your overall compliance status.

questions.question: A startup with three subscriptions is told to adopt management groups. A skeptic says management groups are only for enterprises with hundreds of subscriptions. What is the correct response?
options: Management groups are only available with an Enterprise Agreement
Management groups require at least 100 subscriptions to activate
Management groups give enterprise-grade management at scale no matter what type of subscriptions you might have, and they provide a governance scope above subscriptions
Three subscriptions cannot be placed in a management group
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Management groups give enterprise-grade management at scale no matter what type of subscriptions you might have, and they provide a governance scope above subscriptions. B is wrong — there is no minimum subscription count. A is wrong — all Azure customers can see the root management group. D is wrong — any subscriptions can be organized under management groups.
questions.source_title: Organize your resources with management groups
questions.source_quote: Management groups give you enterprise-grade management at scale, no matter what type of subscriptions you might have.

questions.question: A team wants to migrate Blueprints to the recommended replacement while keeping definition storage and versioning. Which pairing does Microsoft describe?
options: Resource locks for assignment and Azure DevOps for versioning only
Policy initiatives for assignment and Blueprints for versioning
ARM templates alone, which provide deny assignments natively
Deployment Stacks for assignment and lifecycle management, plus template specs or a Git repository for definition storage and versioning
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Microsoft recommends Deployment Stacks as the replacement, providing grouping, lifecycle management, and deny assignments, and notes you can publish definitions as template specs or store them in a Git repository to take advantage of versioning. B is wrong — Blueprints is retiring, not a versioning store. C is wrong — plain ARM templates do not provide deny assignments. A is wrong — resource locks do not group or lifecycle-manage deployments.
questions.source_quote: Depending on your needs, you can also publish your definitions as template specs or store them in a Git repository to take advantage of versioning.
